lesson.title: Reading Radical Expressions: Index, Radicand, and Beyond Square and Cube Roots
lesson.summary: A radical expression generalizes square roots and cube roots to any index, using the index to say which power the root is undoing and the radicand to say what value is underneath.
lesson.body:
Square roots and cube roots are the two most common examples of a broader family called radical expressions. A general radical is written with the root symbol, a small number called the index tucked into the crook of the symbol, and the quantity underneath called the radicand. The index tells you which power the root is meant to undo: an index of 2 undoes squaring, an index of 3 undoes cubing, an index of 4 undoes raising to the fourth power, and so on. By long-standing convention, the index 2 is left off entirely, which is why the square root symbol has no visible small number even though it technically means index 2.

This framework makes it possible to work with roots beyond square and cube roots using the exact same logic you already built. To evaluate the fourth root of 16, look for a number that produces 16 when raised to the fourth power. Since 2^4 = 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 = 16, the fourth root of 16 equals 2. Similarly, the fifth root of 32 equals 2, because 2^5 = 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 = 32.

Radical expressions can also contain variables and more complicated radicands, not just plain numbers. An expression like the cube root of the quantity x plus 5 is a perfectly valid radical expression, but it cannot be simplified into a cleaner form unless x plus 5 happens to be a perfect cube for the value of x in question. Recognizing when a radicand is or is not a nice perfect power is a skill in its own right, one you will sharpen further when simplifying radicals in the next lesson.

The index also controls which real numbers are allowed as inputs, and this is where the square root and cube root lessons come back into direct play. An even index, like 2 or 4, behaves like square roots: it requires a nonnegative radicand to produce a real number result, because no real number raised to an even power can be negative. An odd index, like 3 or 5, behaves like cube roots: it accepts any real radicand, positive, negative, or zero, because raising a negative number to an odd power keeps the result negative. So the fourth root of -16 is not a real number, for the same underlying reason the square root of -16 is not a real number, while the fifth root of -32 is a real number, equal to -2, because (-2)^5 = -32, for the same underlying reason cube roots handle negatives comfortably.

Thinking of square roots and cube roots as two instances of this one general pattern, rather than as two unrelated rules to memorize, makes it much easier to extend your understanding to any index you encounter later, and it sets up the vocabulary, index and radicand, that the rest of this unit relies on.

It also helps to notice what the coefficient in front of a radical means, since radical expressions often appear with a number multiplied against the root, like 3 times the square root of x plus 5. That leading 3 is not part of the radicand and is not affected by the index at all, it simply multiplies whatever value the radical evaluates to. Keeping the coefficient, the index, and the radicand as three clearly separate pieces of the expression is exactly the habit that makes simplifying radicals, the next skill in this unit, much more manageable.
